extracted.intended_audience: writers and creative-writing workshop participants (fiction and narrative nonfiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and exercises for narrative craft: use of repetition, adjectives/adverbs, verb person and tense, passive voice, and point of view/voice. Includes classroom exercises and critiquing prompts to develop these skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of a noun, verb, or adjective used deliberately in a passage (a noticeable word, not invisible ones like was, said, did).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition can be comic or devastating: repeated phrases gather weight and meaning (Mr. Micawber example). A single repeated word can act like a hammer blow (Dickens’s 'staring' example). Exercise: write a paragraph (150 words) including at least three repetitions of a noticeable word. In critiquing, listen for whether readers notice the repetition and how it functions emotionally and structurally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of events in a story: happenings that echo one another across a work (involves the whole of a story or novel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural repetition includes foreshadowing and images/themes introduced early that return throughout (Jane Eyre first chapter example). It functions like musical recapitulation and development. Exercise: write a short narrative (350–1000 words) where something said or done is later echoed or repeated in a different context/scale/with different people. For memoirists: be aware of existing life patterns rather than forcing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique repetitions' effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: When critiquing pieces that use repetition, concentrate on how effective the repetitions are and whether they are obvious or subtle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Were you comfortable deliberately repeating words/constructions/events? Did comfort increase while doing it? Did repetition bring out a particular feeling-tone, subject matter, or style? Evaluate whether repetition enriches meaning or becomes distracting/expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives and adverbs: use sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives and adverbs are rich and nourishing; they add color, life, immediacy — they cause obesity in prose only when used lazily or overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the quality an adverb indicates can be put in the verb (they ran quickly = they raced) or the adjective’s quality can be put in the noun itself (a growling voice = a growl), the prose will be cleaner, more intense, more vivid. Adopt a watchful attitude and careful choice of adjectives/adverbs; narrative prose needs more muscle than fat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root out qualifiers ('ticks')
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers habitually use softening qualifiers—adjectives and adverbs such as rather, a little, kind of, sort of, just, very—which weaken their words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify your favorite qualifiers (examples: kind of, sort of, just, a little, very) and remove them. The qualifier 'fucking' used as an intensifier in narrative is singled out as particularly weakening; allowed in dialogue/interior monologue occasionally but damaging in narrative voice. Dig qualifiers out right away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overused/meaningless modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some adjectives and adverbs have become meaningless through overuse (e.g., great, suddenly, somehow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Great' seldom carries weight; 'suddenly' becomes a mere transition device; 'somehow' betrays lazy plotting (nothing happens 'somehow'). Replace or remove these lazy modifiers; take responsibility for events in the story. Ornate or far-fetched adjectives can force the reader to stop to see the connection — effective sometimes but risky in narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected adjective as stylistic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscious stylists may use adjectives in surprising, poet-like relations to nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mannerism can be effective but in narration it risks stopping flow. Ask: Do you want to stop the flow? Is it worth it? Use sparingly and knowingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chastity exercise (no adjectives/adverbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write descriptive narrative prose (200–350 words) without adjectives or adverbs (no dialogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: give vivid description using only verbs, nouns, pronouns, and articles; adverbs of time may be used sparingly. Critiquing: ask whether the piece improves with selective adjectives/adverbs, notice which devices and usages you were forced into (verb choice, simile, metaphor). This exercise 'enlightens, chastens, and invigorates.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of the verb (nonfiction rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonfiction, except for autobiography, has to be written in the third person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To write about Napoleon or a bacillus in the first person is to write fiction. Memoir/autobiography are exceptions because the 'I' is the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons available in fictional narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional narrative persons available are first singular (I) and third singular (she, he), with limited use of first and third plural (we, they); second person (you) is justifiably rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person creates a fictional self distinct from the author; limited third (limited to one character's perceptions) is tactically identical to first person. Choosing person affects voice and requires different imaginative energy from writer and reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change person when story is stuck
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of whether to write in first or third person can be crucial; some stories that get stuck in one person need switching to the other to proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story is stuck in first person, try moving it to third person (or vice versa). Keep the possibility of changing person in mind when narration becomes stuck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb tenses: general properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Past tense and present tense express continuity and temporal relations differently: the past tense handles priority/subsequence easily; present tense tends to cling to the present and is less flexible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract discourse is generally in the present tense. Present-tense narration persuades readers it's 'more real' because it sounds like eyewitness narration; past-tense narration allows continual referring back and forth in time and space and therefore a larger field of vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present-tense narration: effects and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Present-tense narration is focused on action in a single time/place and tends to set up an artificial, permanent emergency; it persuades of immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use present tense when tight focus and immediacy suit the material (fast-paced action, a writer who 'sees' action like film). Be aware it narrows field and can make narrative sound cool, flat, or similar across works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past-tense narration: effects and affordances
rubrics_metrics.description: Past-tense narration allows access to time before and after the moment described, giving continuity, variety, and depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The past tense shows a wider 'field' (compared to present's flashlight vs sunlight analogy). It permits temporal mobility and complexity that the present tense resists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uncontrolled tense-switching ('two-timing')
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent, unmarked switching between past and present tense will likely confuse the reader about sequence and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you change tense within a story, do so deliberately and signal it (line break, chapter break, other markers). Make sure you know why you’re changing tenses and carry readers effortlessly with you; don’t maroon them in temporal confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screenplay tense/voice note
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenplays appear in the present tense but are actually in the imperative voice — instructions describing what is to happen onscreen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screenplay lines are not descriptions but directions to actors, camera, props, etc. (example: “Dick grins at Jane, fires. Blood spatters lens. CU: Spot falls dead.”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive voice: cautious use
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive constructions are widely used in academic and business English; they are indirect and can make thoughts/deeds seem as if nobody took responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers who want to take responsibility are wary of passive voice. If your style has been corrupted by academese/business English, root out misplaced passives. Where passive belongs, use it freely; it is one of the verb’s useful versatilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view and voice (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view (POV) is the technical term for who is telling the story and their relation to it; voice refers to the narrating voice and is pragmatically treated here as intertwined with POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POV and voice determine what can be shown/known/told. Treat them as interdependent choices that shape narration; study different POVs and their effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliable narrator expectation (nonfiction) / unreliable narrator (fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In nonfiction/memoir we normally expect the author/narrator to be reliable; in fiction unreliable narrators who misrepresent or misinterpret often tell us about themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonfiction writers who alter facts knowingly to present a superior 'truth' are judged harshly here; in fiction, an unreliable narrator is a deliberate tactic that reveals character and perspective and can be used to lead readers to infer 'what really happened.'

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person narration (POV)
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narration: the viewpoint character is 'I' and is centrally involved; only what 'I' knows, feels, perceives, thinks, guesses, remembers, etc., can be told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reader’s inference about others must come from the 'I' narrator's perceptions. First person creates a distinct fictional self and requires different imaginative energy from both writer and reader. Study masters (e.g., Grace Paley) to see how pitfalls are avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited third-person narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited third-person: viewpoint character is 'he' or 'she' and narration is limited to that character’s perceptions, feelings, knowledge, and guesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactically identical to first person in its limitation and authentic feel; shifts between limited viewpoints are possible but usually signaled and not too frequent. Limited third is the predominant modern fictional voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involved author / omniscient narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Involved-author (omniscient) narration: story is not told from within a single character; the narrator may tell what anyone is thinking and make judgments the characters cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This storyteller voice knows the whole story and is versatile and manipulable; it is historically common and can be flexible and complex, though potentially open to abuse. It remains a powerful and difficult voice to use well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detached author / objective (camera-eye) narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Detached-author (fly-on-the-wall, camera-eye, objective narrator): no viewpoint character’s mind is entered; the narrator reports only what a neutral observer could infer from behavior and speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values and judgments are implied indirectly rather than stated. This cool voice is useful for writers who must avoid manipulating reader responses overtly; moving a reader with this voice is a strong achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer-narrator (first- or third-person)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observer-narrator: narrator is one of the characters but not the principal actor; the story is about someone else that the narrator witnessed and wants to tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In first-person observer the narrator uses 'I' but tells a story that is not about them; in third-person observer the viewpoint is a limited third narrator who witnessed events. Both tactics offer a witnessing stance distinct from central first-person narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiquing person/tense choices (The Old Woman exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: When critiquing versions of the same scene written in different person/tense combinations, focus on the ease/awkwardness of time shifts and how well suited the chosen tenses and pronouns are to the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare versions (Version One: single person/tense; Version Two: opposite person and swapped tenses for now/then). Consider which pronoun/tenses work best, whether there is much difference between versions and what that difference is. Use these observations to learn how person and tense affect telling, feeling, and wording.
